{"id": "72:1/q09", "question": "What does ٱسْتَمَعَ imply and what is its unstated object?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q09/p1", "position": "The jinn deliberately listened to the Qur'an, whose object is omitted because their following words supply it.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur and Alusi supply Qur'an from the sequel and 46:29; Bursevi distinguishes intentional listening from mere hearing; Biqai stresses exceptional attention; Asad includes acceptance of revelation. Qurtubi instead supplies the Prophet as the object from context; Samin says min al-jinn modifies nafar."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q10", "question": "Why did the jinn seek out this recitation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q10/p1", "position": "Heavenly news was blocked by guards and meteors after Muhammad's mission, so jinn or Iblis's envoys searched for the cause and found his recitation.", "reasons": "Muqatil says heaven had been unguarded between Jesus and Muhammad; Suddi says guarding accompanied a prophet or manifest sign. Farra, Ibn Abbas reports, Mawrdi, Qurtubi and Durr describe search across regions. Suddi has Iblis smell soil to locate Mecca; Qurtubi reports that jinn formerly added nine false words to each true heavenly word. The Taif people first feared the heavens had perished until Abd Yalayl advised checking the fixed stars. Razi and Qurtubi explain that those pelted may be jinn called devils because of rebellion."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q11", "question": "Where and under what circumstances did the jinn hear the Prophet?", "turns_on": "The Ibn Abbas report of an unnoticed hearing and the Ibn Masud reports of an instructed visit, including conflicting accounts of Ibn Masud's presence.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q11/p1", "position": "They encountered him at Batn Nakhlah near Ukaz or Tihama, usually while he recited in the dawn prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas accounts describe travel toward Ukaz with companions, an unnoticed dawn recitation and return to their people; Muqatil places the group at night before finding dawn prayer. Ibn Ishaq puts it after Taif. Zajjaj relates 46:29, where some ask the others to be silent. Wahidi Basit also reports a night prayer and their affectionate crowding. Tirmidhi grades Ibn Abbas's report hasan sahih; Tabrisi cites both Sahihs."}, {"id": "72:1/q11/p2", "position": "In a summoned encounter, he went to the jinn at Mecca or al-Hajun and recited to them; Ibn Masud traditions vary over whether he accompanied him.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda names al-Hajun; Ibn Masud reports a divine order, jinn caller, boundary line, jinn like partridges or Zutt, traces and fires, and a tree testifying to prophethood. One route says Ibn Masud was absent that night and saw traces later; another places him at the line. Bayhaqi notes sound reports support absence but other routes place him there. Jinn requested provisions of bones and dung. Tabaṭaba'i records a separate pledge of seventy-one thousand at a date-palm valley."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q12", "question": "Did Muhammad see or intentionally recite to the listeners in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse describes the unobserved first hearing or an instructed encounter, and how Ibn Abbas and Ibn Masud's reports are weighed.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q12/p1", "position": "No; the jinn heard an ordinary recitation without his seeing or addressing them, and revelation informed him afterward.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas's report says neither sight nor direct recitation; Razi argues that otherwise the Prophet would not attribute knowledge to revelation. Qurtubi cites the wording istamaʿa, and Biqai, Alusi, Ibn Ashur and Islahi infer the same. Tirmidhi grades the report hasan sahih."}, {"id": "72:1/q12/p2", "position": "Yes, he saw or met jinn and recited directly to them when God directed or summoned them.", "reasons": "Mawrdi attributes this to those citing 46:29 and gives Ibn Masud's ordered recitation. Jishumi reports a seen group of seven from Nasibin, who were sent to others; Qurtubi says the Prophet could see jinn in their own forms. Ibn al-Arabi prefers Ibn Masud's eyewitness evidence over Ibn Abbas's report."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q13", "question": "How many jinn encounters occurred and how is this account related to 46:29?", "turns_on": "Whether the jinn listening in 72:1 and 46:29 is one event, or the reports concern repeated visits.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q13/p1", "position": "This is the same listening event narrated in 46:29-32.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq, Zajjaj, Wahidi, Ibn Jawzi, Razi, Abu Hayyan, Biqai's report from Abu Hayyan, Islahi and Study Quran identify the shared account; Ibn Atiyya says its story was treated there. The jinn's return as warners echoes that passage."}, {"id": "72:1/q13/p2", "position": "There were at least two encounters: an unnoticed first hearing and a later requested recitation; reports about Mecca, Nakhlah and 46:29 may refer to different visits.", "reasons": "Razi and Bayhaqi reconcile Ibn Abbas and Ibn Masud by sequence; Qurtubi reports both orders of Mecca and Nakhlah and Bayhaqi's sequence. Abu Hayyan reports Hira without Ibn Masud followed by Hajun with him; Biqai favors multiple events on hadith evidence and distinguishes Nasibin from Nineveh. Kuranyolu also places a later seen meeting."}, {"id": "72:1/q13/p3", "position": "One encounter can reconcile both reports if Muhammad did not know the jinn's private words, or learned their report only afterward.", "reasons": "Razi proposes that he recited without knowing their words and deeds, or saw believing jinn and later received revelation of what they told their people."}, {"id": "72:1/q13/p4", "position": "The differing accounts may reflect six visits.", "reasons": "Alusi gives this as a way to explain the varying reports and notes dating in the eleventh year of prophethood."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q14", "question": "What did the Prophet recite when the jinn listened?", "turns_on": "The reported identity of the passage heard; the verse itself names only Quran.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q14/p1", "position": "He recited the opening of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq.", "reasons": "Ikrima names the sura; Qurtubi specifies Read in the name of your Lord, 96:1."}, {"id": "72:1/q14/p2", "position": "He recited Sūrat al-Raḥmān.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan, Biqai and Alusi preserve an unnamed alternative report."}, {"id": "72:1/q14/p3", "position": "The omitted object may have been Sūrat Ṭā Hā.", "reasons": "Bursevi lists Taha alongside the Quran and iqra as possible supplied objects."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q15", "question": "How many listeners were there?", "turns_on": "Different transmitted counts and whether reports describe the same gathering or later adherents.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q15/p1", "position": "Seven jinn listened.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq says seven from Nisibin; Mujahid divides them into three from Harran and four from Nasibin and gives names; Qushayri says seven later drew seventy converts. Some accounts locate Nusaybin in Yemen. Abu Hayyan says this count conflicts with Ikrima's twelve thousand."}, {"id": "72:1/q15/p2", "position": "Nine jinn listened.", "reasons": "Muqatil speaks of nine from Yemen alongside nobles from Nasibin; Farra says Iblis sent nine; Zirr includes Zawbaa; Dahhak identifies a Yemeni Nasibin distinct from Iraq's; some versions list all nine names, with spelling variation."}, {"id": "72:1/q15/p3", "position": "Twelve thousand jinn from the island of Mosul listened.", "reasons": "Ikrima's report is preserved by Mawrdi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi; Abu Hayyan asks how it can be reconciled with seven and Alusi observes that nafar then simply means group."}, {"id": "72:1/q15/p4", "position": "Seventy thousand followed the Prophet before dawn on the Night of the Jinn.", "reasons": "Makḥūl distinguishes those followers among jinn and says the passage concerned jinn alone."}, {"id": "72:1/q15/p5", "position": "Seventy-one thousand jinn pledged to the Prophet in a separate date-palm valley account.", "reasons": "The report through Ali lists prayer, fasting, alms, pilgrimage, jihad and counsel; Tabatabai says the manner of their alms and jihad is unknown."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q16", "question": "From where and from which group did the listeners come?", "turns_on": "The different transmitted origins, group affiliations and whether more than one delegation is being described.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q16/p1", "position": "They came from Nasibin, sometimes located in Yemen and sometimes in the upper Euphrates or Iraq.", "reasons": "Thalabi, Baghawi and Nasafi state Nasibin; Dahhak specifies a Yemeni village distinct from Iraqi Nasibin; Asad cites Tabari for upper Euphrates and tentatively suggests Jews from Syria or Mesopotamia. Muqatil also speaks of nobles from Nasibin."}, {"id": "72:1/q16/p2", "position": "They came from Yemen or Tihama.", "reasons": "Muqatil identifies nine Yemeni jinn; Zajjaj reports Yemen as alternative to Nasibin; Iblis's search in some reports targets Tihama."}, {"id": "72:1/q16/p3", "position": "They were a mixed group from Harran and Nasibin.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Zirr and Asim's reports split seven into three from Harran and four from Nasibin; Alusi calls the latter Yemeni."}, {"id": "72:1/q16/p4", "position": "They came from the island of Mosul.", "reasons": "Ikrima's report pairs that origin with twelve thousand."}, {"id": "72:1/q16/p5", "position": "The Meccan visitors were from Nasibin and the Nakhlah visitors from Nineveh.", "reasons": "Qurtubi preserves this distinction; Biqai favors multiple encounters on hadith evidence."}, {"id": "72:1/q16/p6", "position": "They belonged to Banu al-Shaysaban or Shaysaban, Iblis's numerous main troop.", "reasons": "Abu Hamza al-Thumali and later Kashshaf, Razi, Qurtubi, Biqai and Alusi report the tribal identification; spellings vary."}, {"id": "72:1/q16/p7", "position": "Their party was led by Zawbaʿa.", "reasons": "Zirr and Asim name Zawbaa with companions; Itqan supplies a full list of names: Zaw

{"id": "72:1/q17", "question": "What religion did the listening jinn previously follow?", "turns_on": "Different reports and Asad's inference from their later statements.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q17/p1", "position": "They were Jews or followers of Mosaic faith.", "reasons": "Zajjaj records this alternative. Asad infers Mosaic faith from 46:30's mention of Moses and 72:3's rejection of the Trinity, with possible Syrian or Mesopotamian origin."}, {"id": "72:1/q17/p2", "position": "They were polytheists.", "reasons": "Zajjaj records this as the other reported identification."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q18", "question": "What can نَفَرٌۭ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the usual small-group range is a fixed lexical boundary and whether human or male reference is intrinsic.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q18/p1", "position": "A group commonly numbering three to ten, or three to nine.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Tustari, Kashshaf, Qurtubi citing al-Khalil, Baydawi, Nasafi, Biqai, Bursevi and Alusi give the common range; Nahhas says three or more, Jishumi a group of men, Bursevi gives more than three and fewer than ten; Tabatabai cites three to nine. Bursevi cites al-Qamus for fewer than ten and plural anfār."}, {"id": "72:1/q18/p2", "position": "It can denote a group above ten, even up to forty.", "reasons": "Alusi criticizes Hariri's strict limit and cites Shabi's dozen-odd men; al-Mujmal gives nafar and raht up to forty, distinguishing raht's common father. Elmalili and Tabatabai preserve the wider range; al-Mujmal's view is specifically up to forty."}, {"id": "72:1/q18/p3", "position": "It can mean a people or following, without a strict count or male or human restriction.", "reasons": "Alusi and Elmalili cite 18:34 and Imru al-Qays for a people or group, and the verse's application to jinn against a male-human restriction. Ibn Ashur says a human term is analogically extended to jinn, as rijāl in 72:6."}, {"id": "72:1/q18/p4", "position": "It can denote one man or one person.", "reasons": "Kirmāni cites a sound hadith interpreted with this usage; Elmalili accepts even one person and traces the local use to the sense of a man. Ibn Ashur gives one to ten."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q19", "question": "What does ٱلْجِنِّ denote in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether jinn names a hidden nonhuman kind or, in this context, previously unknown human strangers.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q19/p1", "position": "Hidden, rational, accountable beings, usually understood as subtle fiery or airy bodies distinct from humans and angels.", "reasons": "Tabrisi contrasts fire, human clay and angelic light; Baydawi, Biqai, Bursevi, Alusi and Kuranyolu describe intelligence, hiddenness, fire or air. Kuranyolu derives jinn from janna, to conceal, gives singular jinnī, and says Islamic sources class them as a third rational species; Alusi compares singular rūmī. Some can take shapes or be seen by prophets. Kuranyolu cites 55:15 and 51:56."}, {"id": "72:1/q19/p2", "position": "Jinn here may be strangers or beings previously unseen by the Qur'an's first audience.", "reasons": "Asad offers this tentative reading from 46:29-32 and considers them possibly Jews from Syria or Mesopotamia."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q20", "question": "Do jinn exist externally, and what sort of beings could they be?", "turns_on": "Whether scriptural jinn are external beings, bodies, immaterial spirits, or a name without an external referent.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q20/p1", "position": "Jinn exist as bodily beings, subtle or even dense, whose different natures can sustain life and extraordinary acts.", "reasons": "Razi argues division into subtle and dense proves no common essence, as accident categories show; bodies may differ essentially despite shared space and dimensions. He permits life in an atom without bodily structure and unseen dense bodies. Alusi argues subtle fiery bodies could have distinct essences and modern philosophers posit remarkable subtle bodies. Qurtubi says all created things are composite and rejects physicians' denial; Kuranyolu describes fire-created conscious agents. Razi also reports and rejects the objection that dividing bodies into subtle and dense presupposes a shared essential bodily reality."}, {"id": "72:1/q20/p2", "position": "Jinn are independent noncorporeal lower spirits of many good and evil kinds, able to know, perceive and influence bodies.", "reasons": "Razi reports ancient spiritualists: lower spirits respond faster but are weaker than celestial spirits; independent substances attach first to air then dense bodies, analogized to the soul's fine vapor from the heart. Qashani portrays earthly souls in subtle elemental forms, some philosophers calling them suspended images; prophets and saints attest them. Baydawi, Bursevi and Alusi report this theory."}, {"id": "72:1/q20/p3", "position": "Jinn are departed human souls that can attach to and help similar living souls.", "reasons": "Razi reports good helpers called angels and inspiration, evil helpers devils and whispering; Baydawi mentions separated souls. Alusi says this conflicts with the Salaf and the apparent Quran and hadith."}, {"id": "72:1/q20/p4", "position": "Many philosophers deny external jinn, treating Ibn Sina's airy shape-changing animal as a definition of a name.", "reasons": "Razi and Alusi distinguish Ibn Sina's nominal definition from affirmation of an entity; Bursevi reports broad philosophical denial. Alusi calls denial of external existence clear unbelief; Qurtubi rejects physicians who infer non-eating simple substances."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q21", "question": "Must bodily structure exist for jinn to live and act?", "turns_on": "Whether observed dependence of life on structure establishes rational necessity.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q21/p1", "position": "No; life and power can inhere in an individual atom without an organized body.", "reasons": "Ashari and most followers deny structure as a condition. Razi argues one life cannot inhere in many substrates; assigning lives to all dependent parts creates circular dependence, and miracles can break observed regularity. Thus God can grant an atom knowledge and power."}, {"id": "72:1/q21/p2", "position": "Yes; life disappears when bodily structure is broken and persists while it remains.", "reasons": "The Muʿtazilites infer necessity from observed destruction of living structure; Razi objects that observation cannot settle unobserved possibilities."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q22", "question": "How may present jinn remain unseen?", "turns_on": "Whether perception follows necessarily from sound senses and ordinary conditions.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q22/p1", "position": "Even a dense visible body need not be perceived when ordinary conditions for seeing are met.", "reasons": "Ashari allows nonperception; Razi cites distant objects appearing small despite equal conditions for all parts and circularity if seeing one part depends on another. He treats habit and rational necessity consistently and notes unseen powerful angels among people. Qurtubi says the Prophet could see jinn and angels in their own forms."}, {"id": "72:1/q22/p2", "position": "Adequate conditions necessarily bring perception of a present body.", "reasons": "Muʿtazilites argue that otherwise nearby drums and horns could pass unnoticed; Razi responds that their distinction between habit and necessity is arbitrary, and their account cannot explain unseen powerful beings."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q23", "question": "How are jinn related to humans and devils, and what is their fate?", "turns_on": "Their ancestry from Iblis or al-Jann, and whether faith grants Paradise in either case.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q23/p1", "position": "Jinn descend from Iblis, as humans descend from Adam; both include believers and unbelievers with reward and punishment.", "reasons": "Hasan says believers of either race are God's allies and unbelievers are devils. Mawrdi and Qurtubi preserve his account; Kuranyolu stresses jinn's free will and accountability."}, {"id": "72:1/q23/p2", "position": "Jinn descend from al-Jann and are distinct from Iblis's devils, which live until his death.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas through Dahhak says jinn die and have believers and unbelievers, whereas devils descend from Iblis; on this view believers enter Paradise through faith."}, {"id": "72:1/q23/p3", "position": "Believing jinn enter Paradise, even if they descend from Iblis.", "reasons": "Hasan states this for Iblis-descended jinn; Qurtubi cites 55:56 as establishing jinn in Paradise; Tustari reports jinn living, eating and drinking in its wild tracts and cites 55:74."}, {"id": "72:1/q23/p4", "position": "Believing jinn descended from Iblis are spared Hell but do not enter Paradise.", "reasons": "Mujahid's view is preserved by Mawrdi and Qurtubi."}, {"id": "72:1/q23/p5", "position": "Jinn eat and drink and are accountable to revelation.", "reasons": "Qurtubi infers eating from their request for bones and cites Quran and Sunna against denial; Tabatabai cites 51:56 for worship and their belief in 72:1-2; Tabrisi infers rationality, Arabic understanding, miracle recognition, moral accountability and missionary activity. Kuranyolu cites 6:130 for prophets to jinn."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q24", "question": "What other powers, limits and appearances are attributed to jinn?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q24/p1", "position": "They are shape-changing hidden agents with limited perception and power, and can interact with humans.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu says they reproduce, travel quickly, see humans, know some otherwise unknown things but not the unseen (34:14), cannot obtain heavenly angelic reports (15:18), and served Solomon (34:12-13). {"id": "72:1/q25", "question": "How have peoples understood jinn or spirit beings?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q25/p1", "position": "Many ancient religious cultures posited good and evil spirit beings, while pre-Islamic Arabs also treated jinn as powers linked to soothsayers.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu surveys Assyrian, Babylonian, Semitic, Egyptian, Greek, Roman, Chinese, Indian, Iranian and Turkic traditions; it describes Jewish and Christian demon beliefs, Arab sacrifices and soothsaying, and the Quran's rejection of making Satan an evil god or jinn divine soldiers (6:100, 51:56). Islahi says Quraysh's soothsaying assumptions made the report pertinent."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q26", "question": "To whom and when did the listeners speak?", "turns_on": "Whether qālū points to their immediate response among themselves or their later address to absent kin.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q26/p1", "position": "They told their own jinn people after returning, inviting them to respond and believe.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq and Mawrdi link their return as warners to 46:29-31; Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi, Ibn Ashur, Tabatabai and Study Quran say the addressees were absent kin. Ibn Ashur says God inspired their warning; Islahi says concern for others follows recognition of truth. Biqai adds possible human allies and the prophetic instruction to convey what one hears."}, {"id": "72:1/q26/p2", "position": "Some spoke to their companions at the scene, asking them to listen.", "reasons": "Zajjaj connects the request to be silent to 46:29; Tabrisi reads qālū as speech of some jinn to others."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q27", "question": "Is the jinn's saying ordinary spoken language?", "turns_on": "Whether the Quran's speech attribution is literal articulation or a representation of their communication.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q27/p1", "position": "It denotes communication of intent figuratively, rather than words pronounced by tongues.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur compares the ant's speech in 27:18 and says the portrayal dignifies Islam by showing callers among both kinds of beings."}, {"id": "72:1/q27/p2", "position": "The jinn understand human language and can give an eloquent verbal account of the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Tabrisi and Razi infer Arabic comprehension; Biqai and Baqli say their description displays eloquence and rhetorical judgment; Islahi says some know both languages."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q28", "question": "What does قُرْءَانًا denote here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q28/p1", "position": "A recited book or heavenly scripture, recited on the Messenger's tongue.", "reasons": "Baydawi calls it a book; Bursevi says it is a book because it is recited through Muhammad; Alusi calls it one of the heavenly scriptures and says the indefinite magnifies its rank."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q29", "question": "How is the hamza of قُرْءَانًا pronounced?", "turns_on": "Pronouncing the hamza fully or easing it.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q29/p1", "position": "The standard mutawātir form pronounces the hamza, preserving the q-r-ʾ consonantal root.", "reasons": "The Qiraat-ER note describes this as the standard reading."}, {"id": "72:1/q29/p2", "position": "Hamza easing smooths the pronunciation to Qurānan without changing the root analysis.", "reasons": "The Qiraat-ER hamza-easing note specifies pronunciation, not a different root."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q30", "question": "What does عَجَبًۭا mean and what makes this Qur'an wondrous?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q30/p1", "position": "It is extraordinary and unmatched in eloquence, arrangement, meaning and guidance.", "reasons": "Mubarrad defines rare without a like; Muqatil calls it mighty and peerless, Ibn Abbas eloquent, and Damghani noble. Mawrdi and Qurtubi distinguish language, eloquent exhortation and greatness of blessing. Wahidi adds clarity and truthful reports; Tabrisi adds its hidden cause, unique form, past and future told by an unlettered man; Zamakhshari, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Biqai, Bursevi, Alusi, Tabatabai and Study Quran elaborate beauty, precise and subtle meanings, inimitability, persuasion and effective guidance. Islahi stresses efficacy, force, wisdom and beauty. Sulami describes enlivened hearts and bodies."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q31", "question": "Why use the noun عَجَبًۭا adjectivally?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q31/p1", "position": "The verbal noun stands for wondrous and intensifies the description.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Biqai, Bursevi, Alusi and Islahi call it emphatic. Samin lists hyperbole, ellipsis for possessing wonder, or an active-participle sense; Biqai says its cause is hidden and its likeness unprecedented."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q32", "question": "What do the jinn's immediate response and later phrases mean?", "turns_on": "The later terms are variously glossed; their separate attributions are preserved in the reasons.", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q32/p1", "position": "They recognized right guidance, believed and returned as callers to their people.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq, Farra, Ibn Qutayba, Ibn Kathir, Durr, Tabatabai and Kuranyolu report their belief, guidance and rejection of shirk; Tabatabai says the guidance covers true knowledge and deeds and genuine felicity. Khattabi and Baghawi quote the jinn's recognition of guidance."}, {"id": "72:1/q32/p2", "position": "In 72:2, rashd can mean right guidance in affairs.", "reasons": "Mawrdi reports the general practical sense."}, {"id": "72:1/q32/p3", "position": "In 72:2, rashd can mean knowledge of God.", "reasons": "Mawrdi reports this alternative."}, {"id": "72:1/q32/p4", "position": "In 72:3, the Lord's jadd means His command, act, remembrance, riches, favor, dominion, majesty, blessing, or God Himself; a grandfather reading reflects ignorance.", "reasons": "Mawrdi attributes command to Suddi, act to Ibn Abbas, remembrance to Mujahid, riches to Ikrima, trial or favor to Hasan, dominion to Abu Ubayda, majesty to Qatada, blessings to Dahhak, God Himself to Said ibn Jubayr, and the grandfather suggestion to an unnamed view."}, {"id": "72:1/q32/p5", "position": "In 72:4, the fool is Iblis or the disobedient ignorant among jinn; shatatan means unjust or false speech remote from right.", "reasons": "Mawrdi cites Qatada's general gloss and Mujahid, Qatada and a Prophetic report for Iblis; Abu Malik says injustice and Kalbi says lie."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q33", "question": "What does the verse teach about Muhammad's mission and the jinn?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q33/p1", "position": "His mission and the Qur'an reach jinn as well as humans; jinn can understand, believe and invite others.", "reasons": "Tabrisi lists rationality, accountability, Arabic competence and miracle recognition; Razi says the disclosure proves the mission includes jinn and jinn are responsible callers; Biqai sees Muhammad's honor and broad following; Bursevi adds tawhid and rejection of shirk. Kuranyolu cites 6:130 and 46:29."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q34", "question": "What lesson does the jinn's response offer Quraysh and the Prophet?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q34/p1", "position": "Their prompt recognition rebukes Quraysh's rejection and reassures Muhammad that receptive listeners can respond.", "reasons": "Qurtubi contrasts jinn discernment with idolaters; Razi says it displays inimitability; Abu Hayyan, Biqai, Islahi and Kuranyolu contrast non-addressee jinn with Arabs who heard repeatedly. Islahi says it awakens Quraysh's honor and consoles the Prophet: rejection lies in hardened hearts, not the messenger or Book; facts of the unseen can guide truth-seekers."}]}
{"id": "72:1/q35", "question": "How does this opening relate to neighboring sūras?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:1/q35/p1", "position": "It contrasts Noah's disobedient people in Sūrat Nūḥ with jinn who readily accepted the final revelation.", "reasons": "Jishumi, Abu Hayyan, Biqai and Islahi draw the contrast with 71:1; Biqai notes Muhammad's shorter time with his people and sees the names al-Jinn and Qul Uhiya as apt. {"id": "72:18/q01", "question": "How is the opening hamza of wa-anna read?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause is read as a dependent fatḥa clause or an independent kasra clause.", "positions": [{"id": "72:18/q01/p1", "position": "The canonical readers open the hamza: wa-anna.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid and al-Fārisī detail the differing fatḥ and kasr patterns in other clauses of the sūra; Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports consensus here, as do al-Qurṭubī, Ibn al-Jazarī, Elmalılı, and Ibn ʿĀshūr. {"id": "72:18/q15", "question": "Is the earth's use as mosque and purifier distinctive to this community?", "turns_on": "How to understand the earlier prophets' ability to pray while traveling, and whether the privilege is place, purification, or community scope.", "positions": [{"id": "72:18/q15/p1", "position": "Prayer across the whole earth is a distinctive privilege of Muhammad's community.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports the common claim that prior communities were restricted to synagogues and churches, citing a sound hadith about the earth as mosque and purifier."}, {"id": "72:18/q15/p2", "position": "The distinct privilege is the combined gift of the earth as mosque and purifier, especially dry ablution.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this answer to the objection that traveling prophets must have prayed outside worship buildings."}, {"id": "72:18/q15/p3", "position": "The comparison concerns earlier communities, not their prophets.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī offers this answer; he says al-Khiḍr, if alive, belongs to Muhammad's community, citing the statement that Moses would have to follow Muhammad if alive."}]}

{"id": "72:18/q17", "question": "What inward meaning is given to mosques and invocation?", "turns_on": "The inward readers apply the mosque and the command to faculties, desires, the heart, or bodily purification.", "positions": [{"id": "72:18/q17/p1", "position": "Mosques signify the perfection of each faculty in submission to the heart, and of heart and spirit, where God's right or attribute appears.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī extends 'mosques' to the perfection of anything."}, {"id": "72:18/q17/p2", "position": "Invoking another means following the ego's aims, caprice, pleasures and desires.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī calls these associations with God according to one's nature."}, {"id": "72:18/q17/p3", "position": "The heart's mosques should be purified for God's Greatest Name alone.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī excludes partial names from the heart's sanctuary."}, {"id": "72:18/q17/p4", "position": "Bodily prostration purifies limbs used to pursue sins and desires.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī says prostration atones and erases sin through the very limbs that carry out action."}]}
